candidate.answerReason: The first number is the irrational number pi. The second and third have reduced denominators incompatible with rational cube and fourth roots, respectively. The fourth equals -10/3.

methods.label: Evaluate exact roots and test the remaining roots
methods.explanation:
Simplify the roots that can be evaluated exactly, and test the other two using reduced fractions.

Since \(\pi>0\), the first number is
\[
\sqrt{\pi^2}=|\pi|=\pi,
\]
which is irrational.

For the middle two numbers, use this fact: if \(p/q\) is a fraction in lowest terms with integers \(p,q\) and \(q>0\), then \(p^n/q^n\) is also in lowest terms for every integer \(n\ge2\). Indeed, a common prime divisor of \(p^n\) and \(q^n\) would divide both \(p\) and \(q\). Consequently, a positive rational number can have a rational \(n\)th root only if its reduced denominator is an integer \(n\)th power.

The second radicand is \(0.8=4/5\). Its denominator \(5\) is not an integer cube, so \(\sqrt[3]{0.8}\) is irrational.

The third radicand is \(0.00016=1/6250\). Since
\[
6250=2\cdot5^5,
\]
its denominator is not a fourth power: in a fourth power, every prime exponent must be divisible by \(4\). Thus \(\sqrt[4]{0.00016}\) is irrational.

For the fourth number, \(\sqrt[3]{-1}=-1\) and \((0.09)^{-1}=100/9\), so
\[
\sqrt[3]{-1}\cdot\sqrt{(0.09)^{-1}}
=-\sqrt{\frac{100}{9}}=-\frac{10}{3},
\]
which is rational. Only the fourth number is rational, choice D.
